title: Two Sizes Up
passage:
Gordon Hoskadale went up two mesh sizes in his cod end – the tail of the trawl – and waited for the small haddock to see themselves out. They did not. A whole spring on, the boxes at the harbour looked much as they had the year before.

“A net is one thing on the deck and another thing down there,” he says. “Tow it, and every mesh pulls long and thin. The hole you measured with your hand is a slot by then. A haddock is round, and it has to get its width through.”

The second change was to the hanging, not the size. He had the same twine turned right round the bag, so the meshes stood as open squares under the drag. The small haddock went out. The plaice were much as before, a flat fish and a stretched mesh being much the same shape. He had not bargained for good fish going out too, on the tows when the square bars ran slack.

– Fiona Hebden, gear pages

questions.rationale: KEY D paraphrases the load-bearing pair of claims the passage actually makes: the mesh sizes went up and nothing changed (“They did not. A whole spring on, the boxes at the harbour looked much as they had the year before.”), and the skipper’s own explanation of why (“Tow it, and every mesh pulls long and thin. The hole you measured with your hand is a slot by then. A haddock is round, and it has to get its width through.”). A stretched mesh keeps its length and loses its width, so a bigger diamond does not hand a round-bodied fish the dimension it needs. No wording is lifted: the passage never uses “narrowed”, “extra size” or “give ... its width” in that arrangement. A is the skim-trap on the time-scale: the passage does say he waited to see what the larger meshes would do, and a reader who takes the opening as one haul supplies a trip where the text has a season. It is refuted by the span that dates the verdict – “A whole spring on, the boxes at the harbour looked much as they had the year before” – a whole spring’s landings, not one trip’s catch. B is the real-event-with-an-invented-consequence trap: the turn is real (“the same twine turned right round the bag, so the meshes stood as open squares under the drag”), and B hangs on it a change in the plaice that the passage rules out in so many words – “The plaice were much as before”. Whatever the plaice had been doing, the turn did not alter it, and the reason the passage gives is the shape they already shared with a stretched mesh, not any new misfit with a square; that second half of B is a mechanism the text never states. A solver who knows that a square mesh sorts round fish better than flat ones will find B plausible as gear knowledge, which is exactly why it has to be checked against the page. C swaps the order of the two changes. The passage sets them out in sequence and names the second one outright – “The second change was to the hanging, not the size” – so the size went up first and the hanging was altered after it, not before. None of A, B or C is true as written, so “best fit” is not doing any work here; each fails against a span a careful reader can point to.

(1996): 'Diamond meshes have the tendency to close when they are stretched... All meshes in front of this zone are stretched and have a reduced mesh opening. Seafish fishing-gear database, 'Square Mesh Cod-ends': 'As the mesh size and shape stays constant, square mesh cod-ends are very efficient at allowing the easy release of small round fish, whilst retaining the larger fish... The square shape of the mesh better suits the cross sectional shape of the round fish for escape through the meshes than the shape of flat fish.'
